Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

could you make a summary of the packet i'm sending about the Northside Laundry Cooperative, not a recommendation or a new plan. It has different kinds of material in it and some bits don't line up neatly, so please say what the documents say and keep a disagreement as a disagreement. The cooperative is in Bellwether, and the packet covers its history, the current service, equipment, money, a possible move, and comments from members and people nearby. I need a useful summary for someone who has not read the packet, not a promotional piece. Please don't make the cooperative sound more settled or successful than the material does.

The first item is a draft history put together by member Rosa Alvarez from old newsletters and two interviews. It says the group began in 2011 after the Riverside laundromat closed, with nine households sharing access to a donated washer and dryer in a church basement. The draft says the cooperative registered as a nonprofit in 2013, but the attached state letter is dated 2014. Don't pick one date as correct; explain that the draft and letter give different years for registration. The history also says the cooperative moved to its current storefront on Alder Street in 2016. One interviewee, Mr. Peter Cho, remembers members doing repairs themselves before they had regular paid staff, while another says a retired building manager did most of the electrical work. Keep those as attributed recollections, not settled facts.

There are current service notes from February through May, with opening hours listed as Tuesday to Saturday, 8:30 a.m. to 6 p.m. The notes say members can use machines by appointment, and walk-ins are accepted when a machine is free. The Tuesday morning slot is reserved for the senior meal program next door, but a note from March says that arrangement was paused for two weeks because the meal program changed its delivery day. Please retain that short pause rather than making it sound like the reservation stopped permanently. The service notes list 46 active household memberships in April, compared with 39 in January. They don't explain whether households on a temporary hold are counted, so don't infer a membership trend beyond those reported figures. The posted wash price is $2.25 per load, with detergent included; the notes say prices have not changed since September 2022.

The equipment inventory lists six washers and five dryers. Two washers, marked W2 and W5, were unavailable on April 11. A later note says W5 was back in service on April 18, but there is no update about W2. One dryer has a recurring door-latch issue, and the repair invoice dated May 6 says the technician inspected it but was waiting for a replacement part. Don't say that the repair was completed. A member reported that the folding table wobbles when the room is crowded. In a staff email, Janelle Reed writes, “we can keep a machine running for now, but that is not the same as having dependable equipment.” This is her wording, and it would be good to keep it or quote it accurately if you use it.

The financial sheets cover the calendar year 2023 and the first quarter of 2024. For 2023 they list $28,400 in wash revenue, $11,900 in member dues and donations, and $36,700 in expenses. The packet does not say whether the revenue figure includes a $2,000 city energy credit shown separately on a receipt. For January through March 2024, the sheet lists $7,150 in wash revenue and $9,600 in expenses, and has a blank where the dues and donations figure would go. Please report the numbers with their periods and don't calculate a surplus or deficit using incomplete categories. A board note says the landlord offered a one-year lease extension at the current base rent of $1,850 per month, with a response requested by June 15. There is also a $325 monthly common-area charge, which the lease summary says can change each January. I can't tell from the packet whether the extension offer includes any change to that charge, so make that uncertainty visible.

Another part is about a possible move to the former post office on Juniper Avenue. The city property office email says it is one of three sites being reviewed for community use and that no tenant has been selected. A cooperative site visit on May 2 recorded a ground-floor washroom, a narrow rear doorway, and space that might fit seven washers if plumbing work is possible. The visit notes say there was no cost estimate and no accessibility assessment. At the May 9 board meeting, two members asked for a full cost comparison before discussing a move, and one member wanted the co-op to ask the city about a longer lease. The minutes say the board “agreed to gather more information.” They do not say the board approved a move, selected the post office, or authorized an application.

Please include the member survey but be clear it was not a full membership vote. Twenty-eight people responded out of 46 active households. Seventeen respondents said evening hours would help them, eleven asked for lower wash prices, and nine mentioned more reliable dryers; respondents could choose more than one answer. Four people wrote that they use the cooperative because they can walk there. Two respondents said they have difficulty using the rear entrance when carrying laundry, but the survey doesn't say whether they meant the current storefront or the proposed site. The comments should not be presented as representative of every member. A neighborhood association letter supports keeping laundry service in the area, while also asking for a quieter vent fan after 9 p.m. The letter doesn't endorse either location.
